content.text: This document serves as an updated architecture review for the billing team, specifically addressing the selection of a queue for background jobs. It supersedes a previous draft shared via chat, indicating a formalization of the discussion.

ai.stableNodeKey: Choosing a queue for background jobs § text#1

content.text: This section outlines the criteria for selecting an option, categorizing them into must-haves and weighted criteria for scoring.

ai.stableNodeKey: Choosing a queue for background jobs › Selection criteria § text#0

content.text: No job is lost when a worker crashes or the service is deployed.
The queue absorbs 1,800 jobs per minute (three times today's peak) without manual intervention.

Monthly cost: 30%

Portability away from our cloud provider: 10%

ai.stableNodeKey: Choosing a queue for background jobs › Options ⨁ Choosing a queue for background jobs › Benefits and trade-offs § table#0

content.text: Option A offers the lowest operational overhead but requires all job handlers to be idempotent, which is a significant development effort. Option B provides advanced queuing features but comes with a substantial operational burden and a lack of team experience. Option C offers strong transactional guarantees for jobs within the billing database but introduces read load on the primary database and doesn't extend to other services.

ai.stableNodeKey: Choosing a queue for background jobs › Options ⨁ Choosing a queue for background jobs › Benefits and trade-offs § text#0

content.text: The catch is that the service delivers each message at least once, so every job handler must be made idempotent before we switch; today only the email handler is.

ai.stableNodeKey: Choosing a queue for background jobs › Decision status § text#3

content.text: The billing service processes approximately 40,000 background jobs daily.
These jobs include rendering invoice PDFs, sending receipt emails, and retrying failed webhooks.
Currently, jobs run in an in-process worker pool.
A deploy or crash results in the loss of queued but unstarted jobs.
Last quarter, 37 invoice emails were lost due to this issue, requiring customers to re-request them.
Peak load reaches 600 jobs per minute during the month-end billing run.

ai.stableNodeKey: Choosing a queue for background jobs › Context § text#0

content.text: Today they run in an in-process worker pool, so a deploy or a crash loses any job that was queued but not yet started.

ai.stableNodeKey: Choosing a queue for background jobs › Context § text#1

content.text: Option C Load Test Results:
Sustained 1,200 jobs per minute with a p95 claim latency of 18 ms on a staging database copy with synthetic jobs.
At 2,000 jobs per minute, primary CPU reached 85% and p95 latency rose to 240 ms.
1,800 jobs per minute was not tested.
Staging copy is approximately a quarter of production size, so results may not be directly transferable.
